idiom_name: getIronSession(req, res, { password, cookieName }) sealing a typed session object into one cookie
implementation_notes: iron-session is the self-contained realization: getIronSession(req, res, options) returns a typed session proxy whose fields are sealed into a single cookie with the password (signed and encrypted, decoded statelessly by the server), and session.save()/session.destroy() write or clear it. Reads are typed as Partial<T>, so the first visit, an expired cookie and a destroyed session all present an empty object - the correct shape for a client-held session. Choose it when a browser cookie is the carrier and the payload must stay opaque; choose the jose variant when other services must validate the token. Note the runtime floor: current releases need a recent Node (v9 requires Node 22.13+ and is ESM-only), and chunk: true exists because a large session can exceed one cookie.
pitfalls: The seal password is the whole trust anchor: rotating it invalidates every live session (the documented way to sign everyone out), and a weak or shared password makes the cookie forgeable.
Unsealing failures (expired, tampered, wrong key) look like an anonymous visitor unless onUnsealError is used to log them.
A session larger than one cookie needs the chunk option or a server-side store; the ~4 KB limit still applies per cookie.
Typed reads are Partial: treating the session as fully populated compiles but throws at runtime for a first visit.

variants.name: Interoperable signed or encrypted JWT (jose)
variants.idiom_name: SignJWT / jwtVerify (or EncryptJWT / jwtDecrypt) over WebCrypto
variants.implementation_notes: The jose variant puts the same conversation state into a standard token: SignJWT plus jwtVerify give a JWS that any other stack can validate, and EncryptJWT plus jwtDecrypt give a JWE when the payload must stay confidential; the module runs on WebCrypto and targets browsers, Node, workers and edge runtimes, which is why it suits API gateways and multi-language systems. Set exp/iat on the builder and verify them on the way in, because a token is a snapshot with no revocation list, and keep the key material stable across instances. Prefer the iron-session variant when the carrier is a browser cookie and the payload may stay private in a proprietary format.
pitfalls: Verify with an explicit algorithms allow-list and the expected key; accepting any algorithm reintroduces the classic JWT confusion attacks.
jwtVerify validates exp/nbf only when they are present - a token minted without exp is effectively permanent.
Keys must be imported once and shared; generating a secret per process breaks validation across a fleet, and rotation requires accepting the previous key.
Cookie-borne tokens inherit the ~4 KB limit and the cookie grammar, so the token should be small even though a header has no such cap.
